36763: A Jewish teacher's account of Jesus as Israel's Messiah, the new Moses-like teacher of Torah, whose kingdom brings Israel's story to its goal and opens it to the nations.
36764: Traditionally Matthew (Levi), the tax collector and apostle
36765: Whoever wrote it was a Jewish follower of Jesus who knew the Scriptures deeply, read them in Hebrew and Greek, and thought like a trained scribe. The Gospel's own picture of the ideal teacher, a 'scribe trained for the kingdom' who brings out treasures new and old, may be a self-portrait.
36766: The text is anonymous. The title 'According to Matthew' is found in the earliest manuscripts that preserve titles, and second-century writers attribute it to Matthew without dissent. Only this Gospel calls the tax collector at the booth 'Matthew' (Mark and Luke call him Levi), which some take as a signature and others as a later tradition shaping the text. Because it seems to reuse most of Mark, many scholars think an eyewitness apostle is unlikely as the final writer; others answer that an apostle could still use a fellow-believer's written account.
36767: Probably Syria, often Antioch; Galilee is a minority suggestion
36768: Antioch had a large Jewish community and an early church of Jews and Gentiles (Acts 11:19-26). The first clear user of Matthew, Ignatius of Antioch (c. 110), fits a Syrian home, but this is an inference, not a datum.
36769: A community of Jesus-following Jews, with a growing number of Gentiles, still arguing with other Jewish leaders about how to be faithful to the Torah after the temple's fall
36771: If the majority dating is right, the temple had been burned in 70 and different Jewish groups were competing to lead Israel's recovery. Matthew's sharp words about 'their synagogues' and about scribes and Pharisees reflect a family argument between Jews over who rightly interprets Moses, not Christians attacking an alien religion.
36772: From Jesus' birth under Herod the Great (who died in 4 BC) to the resurrection, c. AD 30 or 33.
36773: Death of Herod the Great; his kingdom is divided among his sons.
36774: Archelaus deposed; Judea placed under a Roman prefect.
36775: Crucifixion of Jesus under Pontius Pilate (or 33).
36776: Roman armies under Titus destroy Jerusalem and the temple.
36777: Sages at Yavneh (Jamnia) begin reshaping Judaism around Torah study (traditional picture; details debated).
36778: Ignatius of Antioch writes letters that echo Matthew's Gospel.
36779:
Matthew was written into a Jewish world that had just lost its centre. If, as most scholars think, it comes from the 80s, the temple, the place where heaven and earth met and sins were dealt with, lay in ruins. Every Jewish group had to answer the same question: how does Israel stay faithful to God now? The sages who later produced the Mishnah answered by focusing on Torah study and the practice of holiness in the home and synagogue. Matthew's community answered: by following Jesus, who is 'God with us', and whose teaching is the true interpretation of Torah.

This is why Matthew is both the most Jewish Gospel and the one most fiercely critical of other Jewish leaders. It opens with a genealogy from Abraham through David, quotes the prophets with formula citations ('this happened to fulfil...') about ten times, keeps the Sabbath and the temple tax in view, and has Jesus say he came not to abolish the Law and the Prophets but to fulfil them. At the same time it contains the harshest words against 'scribes and Pharisees'. In the ancient world, rival teachers within the same tradition routinely used such language; the closeness of the family makes the quarrel louder.

Roman power stands in the background throughout. Herod, a client king of Rome, tries to kill the infant 'king of the Jews'. Roman soldiers can force a civilian to carry gear for a mile. Roman coins carry Caesar's image. Jesus is executed by a Roman governor on a Roman cross. Matthew ends with the risen Jesus claiming 'all authority in heaven and on earth', the kind of language used of emperors and of Daniel's Son of Man.
36781: Matthew repeatedly says an event happened 'to fulfil what was spoken by the prophet'. For a Jewish reader, 'fulfil' meant more than a prediction coming true: it meant a pattern in Israel's story reaching its full meaning, as when Hosea's words about Israel coming out of Egypt are applied to Jesus, who relives Israel's story.
36783: Pharisees were a popular lay movement devoted to keeping Torah carefully in everyday life, not a clique of legalists. Jesus tells crowds to do what they teach from 'Moses' seat' but not to copy hypocrisy. The quarrel is over interpretation and practice, which Jewish teachers argued about constantly.
36785: Jewish men wore tassels (tzitzit) on the corners of their cloaks as Numbers commands, as reminders of the commandments. The woman with bleeding touches the 'fringe' of Jesus' cloak, the very tassel, and Jesus criticises only those who make theirs extra long for show. Jesus dressed as a Torah-observant Jew.
36787: A Roman soldier could compel a local to carry his pack one mile. 'Go the second mile' turns humiliating compulsion into a free act that shames the oppressor and refuses violent revenge, a practical third way between revolt and resentment.
36789: In an honour-based society, almsgiving, prayer and fasting performed in public earned social credit. Jesus does not abolish these core Jewish practices but tells disciples to do them for the Father who sees in secret, moving the audience from the crowd to God.
36791: Rabbinic language for declaring what is forbidden or permitted under Torah. Jesus gives this teaching authority first to Peter and then to the gathered community, making his followers a school of Torah interpretation under his own authority.
36792:
A first-century Jewish listener would hear Matthew as an Israel story, not a new religion. The opening words, 'the book of the genesis of Jesus Messiah, son of David, son of Abraham', echo Genesis and announce that the long-awaited Davidic king has come. Jesus relives Israel's history: he goes down to Egypt and comes out, passes through water, is tested forty days in the wilderness as Israel was tested forty years, and then goes up a mountain to teach, as Moses did at Sinai. His teaching is organised in five great speeches, which many readers since antiquity have linked with the five books of Moses.

The 'kingdom of heaven' is Matthew's reverent Jewish way of saying 'kingdom of God', avoiding direct use of God's name as many Jews did. It does not mean a place souls go after death. It is the hope of the prophets and Psalms that the God of Israel would reign on earth, put things right, restore Israel and bring the nations to worship him, as the Lord's Prayer says: 'your kingdom come, your will be done, on earth as in heaven'. Jesus is a Jew within Judaism: he wears tassels, teaches in synagogues, pays the temple tax, keeps the Passover, sends his disciples first to 'the lost sheep of the house of Israel', and argues about Sabbath and purity the way Jewish teachers did. What is startling is not that he rejects Torah but that he claims the authority to say what it finally means, and that he presents himself as Immanuel, God with his people, whose presence will remain with them 'to the end of the age'. The final command to make disciples of all nations fulfils God's promise to Abraham that all the nations would be blessed through his seed.
36793: Son of David, son of Abraham
36794: A genealogy and birth stories show Jesus as Israel's true king and God-with-us, threatened by a Roman client king.
36796: Baptism in the Jordan and forty days of testing show Jesus as the faithful Son where Israel had faltered.
36798: The Sermon on the Mount gives the kingdom's way of life as the fullest meaning of the Law and the Prophets.
36800: Healings, mission to Israel's lost sheep and parables reveal the kingdom's hidden, growing presence.
36802: Peter confesses Jesus as Messiah; Jesus speaks of his assembly, forgiveness and the way of the cross.
36804: Jesus enters the city as king, clashes with its leaders and foretells the temple's fall and the final judgment.
36806: Jesus dies as 'King of the Jews', rises, and sends his disciples to all nations with his abiding presence.
36833: God's reign, coming from heaven to earth; Matthew's reverent equivalent of 'kingdom of God'.
36835: Right living in covenant faithfulness to God and neighbour, and God's own putting-right of the world.
36837: To fill full, to bring to intended completion; used of Scripture and of the Law.
36839: The gathered people of God; in the Greek Old Testament it translates the Hebrew qahal, Israel assembled.
36840: Matthew reuses most of Mark's story, often shortening narratives and adding large blocks of teaching.
36841: Jesus answers each temptation with Deuteronomy, and the mountain teaching recalls Moses giving Torah.
36842: The risen Jesus' claim to all authority echoes the Son of Man receiving dominion over all peoples.
36843: James closely echoes the Sermon on the Mount on trials, mercy, oaths and doing the word.
36844: The opening phrase and the closing mission to all nations frame the Gospel with the promise to Abraham.
36845: Matthew presents Jesus as Messiah, son of David, Immanuel and the authoritative interpreter of Torah, worshipped by the magi and the disciples. Jewish readers today often value Matthew as evidence that Jesus was a Torah-observant teacher close to the Pharisees' own debates, while disagreeing that he was the Messiah, since the messianic age of peace has not visibly come. Christians read the abiding presence ('I am with you always') as the climax: the God who dwelt with Israel now dwells with his people through the risen Jesus.
36846: The kingdom of heaven means going to heaven when you die
36847: Many sermons and gospel tracts read 'kingdom of heaven' as the place believers go after death, so that entering the kingdom means securing a place in heaven by trusting Jesus.
36848: In Second Temple Judaism 'heaven' was a reverent stand-in for God's name. The kingdom of heaven is God's rule, coming on earth as in heaven, the hope of Israel's prophets. Jesus announces it as 'at hand', prays for it to come, and speaks of the 'renewal of all things'. N. T. Wright, Scot McKnight and Amy-Jill Levine all stress this this-worldly, Israel-centred meaning.
36849: Careful evangelical scholars largely agree. Jonathan Pennington argues that Matthew's 'heaven' language is not merely a substitute for 'God' but contrasts God's realm with the present earthly order, while still expecting heaven and earth to be united. D. A. Carson and others note that the kingdom does include life beyond death and final judgment. The real gap is between popular preaching and scholarship, not between scholarly camps.
36850: If the kingdom is only an afterlife destination, the Sermon on the Mount becomes optional ethics. If it is God's reign breaking in now, Jesus' teaching on enemies, money and mercy becomes the shape of present discipleship.
36851: The Pharisees were legalists trying to earn salvation
36852: Pharisees are often presented as the archetypal religious legalists who thought they could earn God's favour by rule-keeping, the opposite of grace.
36853: E. P. Sanders showed from Jewish sources that Judaism understood obedience as the response to God's prior gracious election and covenant ('covenantal nomism'). Pharisees were respected popular teachers who sought to make holiness possible for ordinary people. Matthew's woes are prophetic rebukes of hypocrisy within a shared tradition, using the same harsh conventions found in the prophets and at Qumran. Amy-Jill Levine warns that the stereotype has fed Christian contempt for Jews.
36854: Scholars such as D. A. Carson, Simon Gathercole and Stephen Westerholm accept that Judaism was not crudely 'works-righteousness' but argue that Jewish texts also expected final judgment according to deeds and that some groups did trust their own Torah observance. They note that Jesus does denounce real failings. Both sides agree the critique is of hypocrisy and misplaced priorities ('justice, mercy and faithfulness'), which Christians are equally prone to.
36855: Reading the Pharisees as a foil lets Christians miss that the warnings are aimed at religious insiders like themselves, and it has fuelled antisemitism.
36856: 'His blood be on us' as a curse on the Jewish people
36857: For centuries some Christians read the crowd's cry before Pilate as the whole Jewish people accepting guilt for Jesus' death for all generations.
36858: Matthew describes a particular Jerusalem crowd stirred up by a few leaders. Many scholars read 'on us and on our children' as Matthew's grim interpretation of the generation that saw Jerusalem fall in 70. Within the Gospel, Jesus' blood is the 'blood of the covenant poured out for many for the forgiveness of sins', so the line may carry an unintended irony of grace. The Jewish Annotated New Testament discusses its tragic history of use.
36859: Evangelical commentators such as Craig Keener and R. T. France firmly reject any collective or perpetual Jewish guilt, a position also stated in Catholic teaching since Nostra Aetate (1965). Some still hold that the verse speaks of real responsibility by those leaders and that crowd. The debate is about the historical sense, not about blaming Jews today.
36860: This verse was used to justify persecution. Reading it in context protects both the text and Jewish neighbours.
36861: For a community cut off from the temple and in painful dispute with fellow Jews, Matthew said: you have not left Israel's story; in Jesus its Messiah has come, God is with you, and your calling is to live out Torah's heart and bring the nations to Israel's God.
36862: Matthew calls readers to a practical righteousness shaped by the Sermon on the Mount, a church that forgives and restores, and humility about religious hypocrisy. It also invites Christians to read Jesus as a Jew and to repent of using this Gospel against Jewish people.
36863: A fast, urgent announcement that Jesus is the Messiah and Son of God whose royal power is revealed above all in suffering and the cross.
36865: John Mark was a Jerusalem believer whose mother's house hosted the church, a cousin of Barnabas, a sometime companion of Paul and later, according to 1 Peter, with Peter in 'Babylon' (Rome).
36866: The Gospel is anonymous. Papias, writing in the early second century and quoted by Eusebius, reports that Mark was Peter's interpreter. Because Mark was a minor figure, many scholars think the attribution is unlikely to be invented. Richard Bauckham argues that Peter's perspective shapes the story; others think Mark gathered community traditions and that the link to Peter cannot be confirmed.
36867: Traditionally Rome; some scholars propose Syria or Galilee
36868: Latin loan-words (such as legion, centurion, denarius) and the explanation of Jewish customs suggest a non-Palestinian, possibly Roman, audience, but Latin military terms were used across the empire.
36869: A largely Gentile church, with Jewish members, needing to understand a crucified Messiah
36871: Around the time of Nero's persecution (64) or the Jewish War (66-70), believers faced suffering and possibly betrayal. Mark tells them that the way of the Messiah is the way of the cross, and that following him means taking up their own.
36872: From John the Baptist's ministry to the empty tomb, roughly the last one to three years of Jesus' life.
36873: Priene calendar inscription celebrates Augustus' birthday as the beginning of 'good news' (euangelia) for the world.
36874: Claudius expels Jews (and Jewish Christians) from Rome after disturbances.
36875: Great Fire of Rome; Nero blames and executes Christians.
36878:
Mark is the shortest and, on most scholars' view, the earliest Gospel. Its Greek is plain and vivid, full of 'immediately' and present-tense storytelling, as if meant to be performed aloud, which is how almost everyone would have met it. The whole account can be read in under two hours.

Its first line is a political announcement. In the Roman world 'gospel' (euangelion) meant good news of a victory or of an emperor's birth or accession. A famous inscription from Priene in Asia Minor called the birth of Augustus the beginning of good news for the world, and emperors were called sons of a god. Mark begins: 'The beginning of the good news of Jesus the Messiah, the Son of God.' He then quotes Isaiah's promise that God himself would return to Zion to rescue his people. The good news is both Israel's hope and a rival claim to Caesar's.

The likely setting was dark. If Mark was written in Rome after 64, believers had been burned and crucified by Nero. If it was written near Syria or Galilee during the Jewish War, Jerusalem was under siege and false messiahs were appearing. Either way, the Gospel's long passion narrative and its warnings about persecution, betrayal and 'the abomination of desolation' would have hit home.
36880: Corpse impurity, skin disease and bodily discharges made a person ritually impure, which mainly restricted temple access; it was not the same as sin. In Mark, impurity does not spread to Jesus; instead his holiness spreads outward and heals the source. Matthew Thiessen argues Jesus is not abolishing purity law but defeating the forces of death it marks.
36882: Mark pauses to explain hand-washing and Pharisaic practice, which suggests many of his hearers were not Jewish. He also translates Aramaic words like 'talitha koum' and 'ephphatha', keeping Jesus' own voice.
36884: A local Jewish gathering for reading and teaching Scripture and prayer, and a village meeting place. Jesus' public work begins in the Capernaum synagogue on the Sabbath, inside Jewish community life.
36886: The demon-possessed man's name 'Legion', the swine (the emblem of the Roman Tenth Legion was a boar) and the drowning in the sea would have evoked Roman military occupation for first hearers, though how deliberate this is remains debated.
36888: Crucifixion was Rome's most shameful punishment, reserved for slaves and rebels. A crucified Messiah sounded absurd. Mark narrates it as a mock coronation: purple robe, crown, acclamation, the title 'King of the Jews', and a lifting up between two others.
36889:
A Jewish hearer would catch at once that Mark opens with Isaiah's promise of a new exodus: a voice in the wilderness preparing the way for the LORD himself to return to Zion. When Jesus proclaims 'the time is fulfilled, the kingdom of God has come near', he announces that Israel's long exile-like waiting is ending and that God is beginning to reign as King, as Isaiah 52 had promised. Jesus chooses twelve, recalling the twelve tribes; feeds crowds in the wilderness like the manna; calms the sea and walks on it as only the God of Israel does in the Psalms and Job; and calls himself 'the Son of Man' from Daniel 7, the human figure who receives the kingdom from the Ancient of Days.

Mark's Jesus is a Jew among Jews. He attends synagogue, sends a cleansed leper to the priest with the offering Moses commanded, affirms the Shema as the greatest commandment and praises a scribe who agrees with him as 'not far from the kingdom'. His actions in the temple echo Jeremiah and Isaiah: the temple was meant to be a house of prayer for all nations. The great surprise is that the Messiah's kingdom comes through suffering, as with Isaiah's servant who gives his life 'as a ransom for many', and that Mark's first human to confess him Son of God is a Roman centurion at the cross. For Mark's mixed audience, this tied their suffering to Israel's own history of faithful suffering under empires, from Daniel to the Maccabees.
36891: John the Baptist announces the coming one; Jesus is baptised, named Son, and tested in the wilderness.
36893: Jesus proclaims the kingdom, heals, exorcises and forgives sins, stirring wonder and opposition.
36895: The kingdom grows like seed; Jesus stills storms, frees the possessed and raises the dead, yet disciples misunderstand.
36896: On the way to the cross
36897: Peter confesses Jesus as Messiah; three times Jesus foretells his death and teaches servant leadership.
36899: Jesus enters the city, acts against the temple, debates its leaders and warns of its coming destruction.
36901: Anointing, last supper, arrest, trials and crucifixion reveal Jesus as Son of God in his death.
36903: The women find the tomb empty and flee in fear, leaving hearers to answer the call to follow.
36927: A public announcement of victory or a new king; for Mark, that God's reign has arrived in Jesus.
36929: Road, path; Isaiah's highway of return and the road of discipleship to the cross.
36931: At once; used over forty times, giving the story urgency.
36932: Jesus' favourite self-description, drawing on Daniel's heavenly human figure who receives the kingdom.
36933: Mark is framed by Isaiah's new exodus and suffering servant.
36934: The Son of Man and the abomination of desolation come from Daniel.
36935: Jesus' cry from the cross quotes Psalm 22, a lament that ends in praise.
36936: Matthew and Luke both appear to build on Mark's order and wording.
36937: Tradition links Mark with Peter, and 1 Peter names 'Mark my son' in Babylon (Rome).
36938: Mark reveals Jesus as Son of God not mainly through power but through the cross; the centurion's confession comes when Jesus dies. Jewish readers have often seen in Mark's Jesus a Galilean healer and prophet of the kingdom, while noting the Gospel's high claims about him forgiving sins and acting as Israel's God does. Christian readers see Mark's open ending as an invitation: the risen Jesus 'goes before you to Galilee', and each hearer must decide whether to follow.
36939: 'Gospel' means a private plan for getting saved
36940: In many evangelical settings 'the gospel' is summarised as a personal plan: we are sinners, Christ died for us, believe and you will go to heaven.
36941: In Mark, 'gospel' is a royal announcement drawn from Isaiah and from Roman imperial language: God's kingdom has come in Jesus the Messiah. Matthew Bates, Scot McKnight and N. T. Wright argue that the gospel is first about who Jesus is (the king) and what God has done, calling for allegiance (pistis), not only a private transaction.
36942: Scholars such as Thomas Schreiner and D. A. Carson agree the gospel is the announcement of Jesus' kingship but insist that forgiveness of sins, the ransom and personal faith are part of that announcement in Mark itself. Most agree the popular summaries are true as far as they go but can shrink the gospel by leaving out the kingdom, Israel and discipleship.
36943: If the gospel is only a transaction, following Jesus on the way of the cross can seem optional. Mark ties trust and discipleship together.
36944: Jesus abolished the food laws and the Torah
36945: Mark 7:19 ('thus he declared all foods clean') is often read as Jesus setting aside the Jewish law and starting a new religion free of Torah.
